$comment: Build Once launch checklist. Based on the launch checklist in 'Building Real Apps with AI', Book 1 Lesson G16. Each item names the lesson that teaches it. Run: node scripts/launch-check.mjs

items.title: Your architecture is written down (docs/architecture.md)
Your three environments (local, staging, production) are written down (docs/environments.md)
Two-step login (2FA) is on for every account: code host, hosting, database, payments, email, domain
items.how_to_prove: Open the security page of each account and screenshot or note that two-step login is on. List every account by name. Do not paste recovery codes.

items.title: Spend caps are set on every paid service, including AI API keys
items.how_to_prove: For each paid service, note the monthly cap you set and where it is configured. A service with no cap is a FAIL.

items.title: Billing alerts email or text you before a cap is reached
items.how_to_prove: Note the alert threshold for each paid service and paste the confirmation that an alert reached you (subject line and date only).

items.title: Your code repository is private
The main branch is protected: changes arrive only through reviewed pull requests
.gitignore stops .env files from being committed
No .env files are tracked in git (only .env.example)
No secret-looking strings (private keys, live keys, service keys) in tracked files
Local, staging and production each use their own keys and their own database
items.how_to_prove: List each environment and the name (NOT the value) of each key it uses. Show that no key name maps to the same project in two environments.

items.title: Preview deployments point at staging, never at production
items.how_to_prove: Open your hosting provider settings for preview deployments and note which database/API URL they use. It must be the staging one.

items.title: Row-level security is tested with two users (Alice and Bob): Bob cannot read or change Alice's data
items.how_to_prove: Log in as Alice, create a record. Log in as Bob and try to read, edit and delete it. Paste the results (all three must be refused). A test file that does this counts.

items.title: File storage rules stop one user from reading another user's files
items.how_to_prove: Upload a file as Alice. As Bob, try to download it by its path. Paste the refusal.

items.title: Database changes live in a migrations folder in the repo
Nobody changes the production database by hand: every change is a migration file merged to main
items.how_to_prove: Write down the rule you follow and the date you last compared production with your migration files (drift check). Paste the result.

items.title: Package versions are locked (a lockfile is committed)
The latest CI run on main is green
CI has a "required" job that runs always() and fails if any other job failed
Every workflow sets permissions: and every job has timeout-minutes
The AI-assistant guard hook is installed (.claude/hooks/guard.mjs)
The guard is registered as a PreToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json
The guard self-test passes (node guard/selftest.mjs)
Automatic database backups are on
items.how_to_prove: Screenshot or note the backup schedule and retention in your database provider.

items.title: You have restored a backup into a scratch database and checked the data
items.how_to_prove: Restore a backup into a throwaway database. Paste the restore steps and a row count you compared. Record how long it took.

items.title: Rate limits protect login, sign-up, password reset and any costly endpoint
items.how_to_prove: List each protected endpoint and its limit. Paste the response you got when you exceeded it (e.g. HTTP 429).

items.title: Sign-up and password reset are protected by a CAPTCHA or bot check
items.how_to_prove: Note which provider and which forms. Paste proof that a request without the token is refused.

items.title: A privacy policy exists and is linked from the app and the sign-up page
items.how_to_prove: Paste the public URL and where it is linked from.

items.title: Terms of service exist and are linked from the app and the sign-up page
items.how_to_prove: Paste the public URL and where it is linked from.

items.title: Users can delete their account and their data from inside the app
items.how_to_prove: Create a test user, delete it through the app, then check the database and storage: paste the queries showing the rows and files are gone.

items.title: Payment test keys and live keys are separate, and live keys exist only in production
items.how_to_prove: Note which environment holds live keys (names only). Confirm staging uses test mode.

items.title: Payment webhooks verify their signature and reject unsigned calls
items.how_to_prove: Send a webhook request with a bad signature to staging and paste the refusal (e.g. HTTP 400).

items.title: App store requirements are met (if you ship a mobile app)
items.how_to_prove: Paste the store checklist result. If you do not ship a mobile app, write "Result: N/A - web only".

items.title: Error monitoring is on, and a test error showed up in it
items.how_to_prove: Trigger a deliberate test error in staging and paste the event ID/time from your monitoring tool.

items.title: An uptime alert is set up and PROVEN to reach your phone
items.how_to_prove: Point the monitor at a URL that fails, wait for the alert, and note the time it arrived on your phone. Setting it up is not enough - it must arrive.

items.title: A written incident plan says who does what when something breaks
items.how_to_prove: Link the plan file and the date you last walked through it.

items.title: Dependabot is configured (.github/dependabot.yml)
Dependabot alerts and security updates are switched on in the repository settings
items.how_to_prove: Screenshot or note the Settings > Code security page showing both switched on.

items.title: A handoff file (HANDOFF.md) is present for the next session or person
